titre: Getting started: the workshop and your first program
resume: Before writing code, you learn to assemble it, run it and watch it in the workshop, the equivalent of [[atari:Devpac and MONST|amiga:Devpac or ASM-One]]. You discover the shape of an assembly line, a first program and the method for finding your mistakes. [[atari:The Atari ST manual left these tools for the end; here, we start with them.|amiga:Books often leave these tools for the end; here, we start with them.]]

atari-ch01-n1.titre: The workshop and the first program

atari-ch01-cours-atelier.source: Written for 68k Trainer from the Atari ST manual v2 (module 6) and the Féroce Lapin course (lesson 1)

atari-ch01-cours-ligne.source: Rephrased from David Bouchet's EPITA course (structure of a source file) and the Atari ST manual v2 (§ 1.1)

atari-ch01-ex-premier.titre: Your first program, step by step
atari-ch01-ex-premier.introduction: Click Next step to run one instruction at a time: the register that has just changed lights up in yellow, and the explanation of the line appears below the code.

explications.3: `MOVE.W #5,D0` copies the immediate value 5 into D0, which is now `$00000005`, and the PC moves on to the next instruction.
explications.4: D1 receives 3 and D0 does not move, because an instruction only changes its destination.
explications.5: `ADD.W D1,D0` adds the source D1 to the destination D0: D0 = 5 + 3 = 8, and D1 keeps its value.
explications.6: `RTS` takes the return address to [[atari:TOS|amiga:the CLI]] from the top of the stack and hands control back to it.

atari-ch01-ex-premier.conclusion: Registers hold the values, instructions transform them one by one, and the PC moves from one instruction to the next.

atari-ch01-pred-sub.introduction: Answer without running the program, then check. `SUB.W D1,D0` does D0 ← D0 − D1.

q1.enonce: What is D0 at the end?
q1.explication: 10 − 4 = 6: the source D1 is taken away from the destination D0, and the order matters.

q2.explication: D1 is the source of the subtraction: it is not modified.

atari-ch01-exo-completer.enonce: The program adds 2 to D0. Replace the `0` in the first instruction so that D0 is 9 at the end.

atari-ch01-exo-ordonner.titre: Put the program back in order
atari-ch01-exo-ordonner.enonce: The instructions have been shuffled. Put them back in order with the arrows to get D2 = (6 + 2) × 5 = 40. `ADDQ` is a quick `ADD` for values from 1 to 8, and `MULU` a multiplication.
indices: D2 needs a value first, and RTS must be the last instruction.

atari-ch01-exo-ecrire.enonce: Put 100 in D1 and 25 in D2, then subtract D2 from D1 to end up with D1 = 75.
indices: Two `MOVE.W` instructions to load the values.
Subtraction is written `SUB.W source,destination`: the destination receives destination − source.

atari-ch01-exo-autonome.enonce: Compute D0 = 3 × (4 + 5) using only `MOVE` and `ADD`, without `MULU`.
indices: Multiplying by 3 means adding the same value three times: keep a copy in another register.

atari-ch01-cours-deboguer.titre: Two kinds of errors and a method
atari-ch01-cours-deboguer.source: Written for 68k Trainer; method taken from the literature review (explicit teaching of debugging)

atari-ch01-ex-bug.titre: A logic error, tracked down step by step
atari-ch01-ex-bug.introduction: This program should compute D0 = 2 × (3 + 4) = 14. It assembles without errors, but D0 is 7 at the end. Follow the method: hypothesis, step-by-step inspection, check.

explications.5: D1 receives a copy of 7, with no discrepancy so far.
explications.6: This is where the discrepancy appears: D1 becomes 14 but D0 stays at 7, because D1 was doubled instead of being added to D0. The fix is `ADD.W D1,D0`.
explications.7: The program ends with D0 = 7 instead of 14; you fix the first line where reality departed from what was expected.

atari-ch01-ex-bug.conclusion: When you move step by step and predict each line, the first surprise points to the error.

atari-ch01-pred-crash.introduction: This program assembles without errors. Look carefully at the destination address.

choix: it writes $1234 at address $3001 and ends normally
it stops on an address error ([[atari:3 bombs on an ST|amiga:Guru Meditation #00000003 on the Amiga]])
q1.explication: A word is always read and written at an even address. Since $3001 is odd, the 68000 raises an address error, exception no. 3, [[atari:hence the 3 bombs|amiga:hence Guru #00000003]]. The assembler cannot see this: it is a runtime error.

atari-ch01-exo-syntaxe.enonce: This program should put 5 + 7 = 12 in D2, but it does not assemble. Click Check, read the message and fix the faulty line.
indices: The message mentions an unknown instruction.
Addition is written `ADD`, with a single D.

atari-ch01-exo-logique.enonce: This program assembles, but D3 is not 30 at the end as intended. Find the faulty line step by step.
indices: Look at which register changes on the addition line.
In `ADD.W source,destination`, it is the destination that receives the result.

atari-ch01-exo-diese.enonce: We wanted D5 = $1001. The program assembles and runs without crashing, but D5 holds a strange value. Before fixing it, find out what is stored at address `$1000`.
indices: Without `#`, `$1000` is an address, not a value.
At address $1000 you find… the code of your own first instruction.

atari-ch01-bonus-fond.enonce:
[[atari:On the Atari ST, the screen background takes color no. 0 of the palette, which you set by writing a word at the hardware address `$FF8240`, in the format `$0RGB`, each component ranging from 0 to 7: bright red is `$700`.

Paint the background red, then watch the screen change step by step.|amiga:On the Amiga, the screen background takes color no. 0, the `COLOR00` register of the Denise chip, at address `$DFF180`. A color is written `$0RGB`, each component ranging from 0 to 15: bright red is `$F00`.

Since the Copper, a small processor inside the chips, repaints the background 50 times a second with the Workbench color, a single `MOVE` only lasts an instant. So repaint the background red in a loop, until a click of the left mouse button: bit 6 of the byte `$BFE001` then drops to 0. Run the program in Real time and click on the screen to finish.]]
indices: [[atari:A single instruction is enough: a `MOVE.W` of an immediate value to an address.|amiga:A loop: `MOVE.W #$F00,$DFF180`, then `BTST #6,$BFE001` and `BNE` back to the start of the loop.]]
[[atari:`MOVE.W #$700,$FF8240`|amiga:`BTST` sets Z to 1 when the bit is 0: `BNE` loops back as long as the button is not pressed.]]

q1.enonce: Which program turns your assembly text into machine code?
q1.explication: The assembler ([[atari:GENST|amiga:GenAm]] in Devpac, the 68k Trainer one here) translates each instruction into machine code. The debugger is for watching the program run.

choix: the rest of the line is a comment
q2.explication: `#` marks an immediate value. Without `#`, 5 would be memory address 5.

q3.explication: The `$` prefix marks hexadecimal and `%` binary; with no prefix, it is decimal.

q5.enonce: In the line `BOUCLE: ADD.W D1,D0 ; total`, what is `BOUCLE`?
q5.explication: A label starts in the first column: it is a name given to the address of the line.

q6.enonce: What is D0 after these two instructions?
q6.explication: 8 + 8 = 16, which is $10 in hexadecimal. Be careful not to confuse $10 (sixteen) with 10 (ten).

q7.enonce: What is the final `RTS` of our programs for?
choix: To hand control back to [[atari:TOS|amiga:the system]]
q7.explication: [[atari:TOS|amiga:The CLI]] starts the program as a subroutine; RTS returns to the caller.

q8.enonce: In what order does the debugging method go?
choix: Inspection, fixing every suspicious line, check
q8.explication: You form a hypothesis, inspect step by step to find the first faulty line, then fix that line and check.

q9.enonce: [[atari:On an Atari ST|amiga:On a 68000]], a `.W` access at an odd address causes…
q9.explication: [[atari:The number of bombs|amiga:The Guru number]] is the exception number: 3 = address error.

q10.enonce: An error reported by the assembler (line underlined in red) is…
q10.explication: The assembler only sees the text: it reports syntax errors. Logic errors and exceptions only show up when the program runs.
